title: Causal Discovery for Irregularly Sampled Time Series
one_liner: When time series have missing chunks and uneven sampling, you must fix the gaps AND find the causal links together, or each mistake poisons the other.
lead: Most causal discovery methods assume clean, evenly-spaced time series. Real data from hospitals and weather stations has holes: a patient skips appointments, a sensor dies for a week. Filling those holes badly breaks causal discovery, and finding causal links wrong breaks gap-filling. ReTimeCausal solves this by alternating: fill the gaps, then update what causes what, then fill again using better causal knowledge. The paper proves this dance actually works.

problem.h2: The tangled knot: gaps and causality confuse each other
paras: In hospitals and weather monitoring, measurements come in at odd times. A blood test happens Tuesday, the next one Friday. A rain gauge breaks for three days. You want to know: does patient A's blood pressure cause their glucose level to rise? Does wind speed cause rain? But half your data is missing.

A naive first attempt: fill in the missing values (guess what happened on Wednesday), then run a standard causal discovery method on the completed data. This sounds reasonable. But the guesses are wrong (you have no idea what Wednesday's reading was), and those wrong guesses twist the causal structure. You find false links that do not exist.

Or try the reverse: ignore the gaps, run causal discovery on whatever data you have. But gaps create phantom patterns. If you measured Monday and Thursday but nothing in between, random noise on those days looks like correlation even if there is no causal link.

callout.html: Mistakes in gap-filling make causal discovery fail, and mistakes in causal discovery make gap-filling fail. You cannot solve them separately.

steps.text: Initialize a causal graph using the available data, gaps and all.
Use kernel smoothing (a method that looks at nearby measurements to guess missing ones) guided by the current causal structure.
Run sparse regression on the filled data, but penalize structures that violate acyclicity (you cannot have A causes B and B causes A).
The algorithm alternates until the gaps and the causal graph stop changing.
The paper proves mathematically that the final graph matches the true causal structure with high probability.

object.h2: The thing being changed: missing data AND causal links, in lockstep
paras: Earlier work treats gap-filling and causal discovery as separate problems. ReTimeCausal couples them: when you estimate a missing value, you use your best current knowledge of causality; when you update causality, you use your best current gap estimates. The object is the pair (filled values, causal graph), and both move together.

hidden.name: Mutual information loss from misalignment
paras: When gap-filling and causal discovery disagree, you lose information. If you think A causes B, your gap-filler will interpolate B's values based on A's history. But if the causal graph is wrong, those interpolations will be biased, and causal discovery will then find a different (wrong) structure. The hidden quantity is this feedback loop: how much information is lost because imputation and causal learning are out of sync.

ReTimeCausal tracks this by measuring how much the imputed values change after each causal update, and how much the causal graph changes after each imputation step. When both stabilize (stop changing), the system has found structural consistency—the imputation matches the causality, and vice versa.

heat.caption: Darker cells show which imputation and causal steps updated together. Consistency improves as the two halves align.

reads.html: Structural consistency means the gap-filling and causal discovery have stopped contradicting each other.

The paper measures consistency via convergence of the alternating optimization; theoretical guarantees ensure the limit point recovers the true causal graph under conditions on the kernel and sparsity penalty.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: alternation breaks the poison cycle
paras: The poison cycle: bad imputation twists causal discovery, which twists the next imputation. Naively, you might think this gets worse and worse. But alternating imputation and causal learning reverses the damage. Here is why.

When you first impute, you make mistakes. When you then learn causality from the imputed data, you do discover some wrong links. But critically, you also learn the structure that is most consistent with the imputed values. In the next imputation step, you use this structure. Even though the structure is not perfect, it is better aligned with the data than a random structure would be, because sparse regression (the algorithm's learning method) chooses the causal links that explain the patterns in the filled data best—any guess is better than no structure at all. The next imputation is less wrong. This reduces the structural inconsistency—the mismatch between what the causal graph says about dependency and what the data actually shows.

Mathematically, the paper proves that this alternating process converges to a solution where the imputed values and the causal graph agree with each other, and under mild conditions (sparse true causal structure, smooth local relationship properties), this solution is close to the true causal graph. Why alternation works: each step pulls the solution toward a state where imputation and causality are in sync, like two gears meshing together. You cannot solve them separately because each mistake in one makes the other worse; by forcing them to improve together, you escape the poison cycle.

stages.s: Use causality to guide gap imputation
Use filled data to refine causal graph

math.h2: The equation: balancing imputation and structure
math.words: The loss combines three terms: a data fit term (how close the imputed values match the observed data), a causal sparsity term (penalize complex graphs), and a consistency term (penalize mismatch between imputation and causal model).
math.equation: Loss = ||Y_obs - Y_impute||^2 + lambda * ||graph_edges||_1 + mu * sum_i || impute_i - predict_i(graph) ||^2
symbols: the guessed values for missing days
count the number of causal links (sparsity penalty)
what the current causal graph predicts for day i

worked.title: Tiny worked example with 3 days and 2 variables
lines: Day 1: measure A=10, B missing. Day 2: measure A missing, B=20. Day 3: measure A=12, B=18.
Guess imputation: A at day 2 = 11, B at day 1 = 19.
Try causal structure: A causes B.

Consistency: Does the causal model A->B predict the filled values correctly? If A and B are causally linked by a simple rule B~0.8*A, then at day 1 the model predicts B~8, but we guessed B=19. The error is (19-8)^2=121. At day 2 model predicts A~12.5, but we guessed 11. Error is (11-12.5)^2=2.25. Consistency penalty: mu * (121 + 2.25) = mu*123.25.

Total loss = 0 + lambda*1 + mu*123.25. The large consistency penalty means this causal structure (A->B) is not consistent with our imputations. The algorithm will either re-impute B to be smaller at day 1, or change the causal structure.

math.note: The algorithm converges when the imputations and the causal graph support each other, which means they are both close to the truth.

charts.title: Naive: impute first, then discover
charts.note: Wrong imputations poison causal discovery from the start.

charts.title: ReTimeCausal
charts.note: Alternation pulls imputation and causality into alignment, improving both.

items.b: High missingness breaks the kernel smoothing.
items.html: If more than 70 percent of data is missing, the kernel cannot see enough neighbors to guess the gaps accurately. The algorithm will still run, but the initial imputations will be poor, and convergence may take longer or get stuck in a bad local optimum.

The algorithm uses linear sparse regression to learn causal links. If the true causality is highly non-linear (e.g., A causes B only when B is above a threshold), the regression will miss it and learn a linear approximation instead.

If an unmeasured third variable causes both A and B, the algorithm will see A and B move together and may incorrectly infer A causes B (or B causes A), even though there is no direct causal link between them.

items.b: Done right: sparse, linear causal structure with missing-at-random data.
items.html: When the true causal graph is sparse (few links), the relationships are approximately linear, and data is missing randomly (not systematically), the theory guarantees ReTimeCausal recovers the true structure.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Generate a synthetic time series with known causal structure (e.g., variable A causes B, B causes C, with no other links). Randomly remove 30 percent of the data points. Run ReTimeCausal and a naive baseline (impute missing values independently, then run standard causal discovery). Measure the accuracy of the learned causal graph against the true graph.
demo.closing: The demo must show that ReTimeCausal recovers the correct causal structure much more often than naive imputation-then-discovery, especially as missingness increases.
